creator: trainbloom
caption:
Hate to burst your bubble (or maybe rings in this case? lol)

But any device that tells you how many calories you burned during a workout is simply not even close to the truth.

(p.s. congrats @sam_sulek , you killed it this weekend)

Devices like the Apple Watch, Whoop, Oura, etc. are great for certain things (e.g. step count, sleep data, recovery)

But they suck for figuring out how many calories you burn

Yes, the technology in these devices has gotten better since this study came out a few years ago…

But the technology isn’t why they’re innacurate

Here’s what the calorie tracking device takes into account to give you an estimate of how many calories you burn:

- Heart rate
- Gender
- Weight
- Age
- Workout type

But what it would take to *accurately* estimate how many calories you burn during a workout is all of that, PLUS 100+ other things that these devices can’t take into account…

Things like your hormone profile and genetics, to even more ridiculous things like the temperature of the room you’re in or how much sleep you got last night…

But that’s okay…

Because knowing *exactly* how many calories you burned in one workout doesn’t really matter

The amount of calories you burn in your workouts is <5% of what you burn in an entire week

So if you’re trying to lose weight, adjusting your calorie intake day by day doesn’t really make any sense

And it would make a lot more sense by just paying attention to your calorie intake and comparing it to how your scale is moving over time

e.g. if you are eating 2,200 calories consistently, and the scale isn’t moving, then 2,200 is around your maintenence and you should either eat below that or increase how many calories you burn in a day to get into a deficit

Study mentioned in reel:
PMID: 28538708

transcript.text: because when I see somebody wearing an Apple watch
and they post it after their workout,
really, you burned 1,500 calories in an hour.
Exactly how inaccurate are these?
Well, lucky for us, Stanford researchers wanted to find out.
They took seven of the most popular wrist worn
calorie tracking devices and put them on people
for a few different workouts to see how accurate they really were.
And the results even shocked the researchers
because although these things were accurate
at measuring things like your heart rate and step count,
when it came to measuring calories,
even the best one was off by almost 30%.
And the worst, off by 93%.
Meaning if a tracker says you burned
1,000 calories during a workout,
you might have only burned a few hundred.
And yeah, technology has gotten better
since this study came out a few years ago,
but the technology wasn't the problem.
The real issue is that these devices only use
about five metrics to come up with that number.
Whereas in reality, there are hundreds
that influence how many calories you burn.
Things these devices can't take into account.
But that's all okay, because knowing exactly
how many calories you burned during a workout
doesn't really matter.
And there are way more important numbers
to pay attention to if you wanna lose weight.

hook.text: Because when I see somebody wearing an Apple Watch and they post it after their workout, really, you burned 1,500 calories in an hour.
hook.template: When I see someone [DOING COMMON THING] and they say [IMPLAUSIBLE RESULT]... really?
hook.whyItWorks: It calls out something millions of viewers do themselves (trusting the watch's calorie number) and the eye-roll 'really?' signals a correction is coming, which opens a gap: is my number wrong too? The reaction split-screen of a recognisable gym guy checking his watch makes the scenario instantly visual, and the big '1500 CALORIES' caption gives the eye a number to snag on.

format.visualLayout: Opens as a reaction (creator on top, gym clip picture-in-picture with bold word-by-word captions), then alternates talking head at a podcast mic with full-screen white motion-graphic explainers (Stanford logo, device line-up, bar charts, metric bubbles).
format.pacing: medium-fast: 8 scene switches in 63s (reaction, talking head, graphic, back and forth), with a new animation or caption beat about every 1 to 2s inside each scene
format.reasoning: A study is dry on its own, so the reel turns every number into a picture: bars for error rates, a full vs nearly empty bar for 1,000 vs a few hundred calories, a flood of words for 'hundreds of factors'. Cutting back to the talking head between graphics keeps a human voice and opinion on top of the data, and the reaction opener borrows a familiar gym moment to set up the myth before busting it.

angle.topic: How accurate fitness trackers are at counting calories burned
angle.angle: Watches are fine for heart rate and steps but badly wrong on workout calories, because they guess from a handful of inputs; and the exact number doesn't matter for fat loss anyway
angle.commonBelief: The calories my smartwatch says I burned are accurate, so I can plan (or eat back) food around them
angle.contrarianTake: Even the best tracker was far off on calories and better tech won't fix it, since hundreds of factors drive real burn; stop chasing workout burn and watch intake against the scale trend instead

myVersion.hook: Your watch says you burned 700 calories in one Zumba class? Sorry, I don't buy it.
myVersion.script:
Your watch says you burned 700 calories in one Zumba class? Sorry, I don't buy it.
Let me explain.
Smartwatches and fitness bands are great at some things. Steps. Heart rate. Sleep.
Calories burned? Not so much.
Research testing popular wrist trackers has found that calorie number can be way off. Sometimes by a lot.
And no, it's not because your band is cheap.
It's because your watch is guessing.
It knows your heart rate, your age, your weight and the workout you picked.
That's it.
It doesn't know your hormones. Your PCOS or your thyroid. How badly you slept. How hot your room was. How much muscle you're carrying.
All of that changes what your body really burns.
So here's the trap I see all the time.
Watch says 500 calories. You think, great, I've earned that extra paratha.
Then you wonder why the scale is stuck.
My advice? Stop eating back your watch calories.
Keep wearing it for steps and sleep. Love that.
But for fat loss, watch two things instead.
What you're eating every single day.
And how your weight is moving over two to three weeks.
Same food, same weight for three weeks? That's your answer. Eat a little less, or move a little more through the day.
Simple. Boring. It works.
